text: Declare, fill, read back; size, memory and indexing.
read back from a[n-1] down to a[0]
One variable holds only its last value. An array keeps every value, and because the index is a variable, a loop can reach any box in any order.
int a[N] has boxes a[0] to a[N-1] . There is no a[N] .
Where / how Starting values global int a[N]; all 0 local int a[N]; garbage = {1, 2} listed values, rest 0
fill(a, a + n, v) first n boxes become v fill(begin(a), end(a), v) every box becomes v
A local array is not zeroed: write = {} or call fill . With many test cases, reset only the first n boxes, fill(a, a + n, 0) , not the whole array each time.

text: Declare big arrays global: they start at 0 and do not overflow the stack. Size with a margin: int a[1005] for n ≤ 1000.
Choose 0-based (a[0..n-1] , loop i < n ) or 1-based (a[1..n] , loop i <= n ) and keep it the whole program. 1-based leaves a[0] free as padding.
Reading past the end (a[n] , a[-1] ) does not crash reliably. It reads a neighbour or garbage, and the bug shows up far away. Starting a reverse loop at i = n prints one value that was never filled.
Tables a[i][j], 3D arrays, and lookup tables.
Think of a table: the first index picks the row, the second the column. Read and print with two nested loops: rows outside, columns inside.

int g[105][105] is 105 × 105 ints ≈ 44 KB. A 3D array a[N][N][N] works the same way with a third loop (P5729). A grid of characters is easiest as string g[N] : read one row per cin >> g[i] , and g[i] [j] is still row i, column j.

Output that is drawn line by line (a display, a histogram) is built row by row: the outer loop is the screen row, the inner loop walks the items. Store fixed pictures in a lookup table and index it (P5730).
Records and counters, pairs and windows, grid walks, transforms and encodings.
Let the index be the thing itself: a position or a value.
cut [2,5] then [4,7]: positions 4, 5 hit twice, still 1
Record: mark[p] = 1 says "position p has property X". Setting a box to 1 twice leaves it at 1, so overlaps are handled for free.
Counter: cnt[v]++ says "saw value v once more". One step per value, no searching.
Subtracting range lengths double-counts overlaps (10 − 4 − 4 = 3, wrong). Marking gives 5. With cut[p]++ instead of = 1 , the box counts how many ranges covered p, and == 0 still means "never cut".
Cost: O(m × L).

Negative values: shift by a constant, cnt[v + 100] ; index i means value i - 100 ; −100..100 needs 201 boxes. Toggles: x ^= 1 flips 0 and 1. Counting the array by value also sorts it: walk the indices in order and print each value cnt times.
Two indices, or a window that slides. self · ✓ · dup self · ✓ dup dup self · dup dup dup self
Every element against every other: outer i , inner j = i + 1 . That visits the upper-right triangle: each pair exactly once, never an element with itself.
Starting the inner loop at j = 0 counts each pair twice and adds every self-pair that passes: wrong = 2 × correct + n. On 3 9 4 8 with |diff| ≤ 1: 2 becomes 8.
n(n − 1) / 2 pairs, O(n²): fine up to n ≈ 5000.
Pairs + a record array: mark every sum first, then ask once per value. A value made by several pairs is still counted once, which is what "how many numbers" questions want (P2141).

title: A window of m consecutive values

text: slide right: add a[6] (green), drop a[2] (dashed)
Recomputing each window costs O(n·m). Sliding costs O(n): the next window = this window + the new right value − the old left value.
Both sources come from row i - 1 : a[5][2] = a[4][1] + a[4][2] = 1 + 3 (orange → green). The zero padding in row 0 and column 0 makes every row start and end with 1 without an if (P5732).

title: Walking a grid with direction arrays

text: Direction becomes a number d ; moving is x += dx[d], y += dy[d] ; turning right is d = (d + 1) % 4 . Spiral rule: go straight until the next cell is outside or already filled (P5731). ↖ ↑ ↗ ← • → ↙ ↓ ↘

Check the bounds before reading g[ni][nj] . Or use 1-based storage with a padding border so every neighbour exists. Marking a fixed shape around each point (a torch's light) is the same loop with a different offset list (P1789).
Grids changed as a whole: rotate, mirror, encode.

column 0 of A, bottom to top = row 0 of B Transform (0-based, n × n) Rule: b[?][?] = a[i][j] Rotate 90° clockwise b[j][n-1-i] Rotate 180° b[n-1-i][n-1-j] Rotate 270° clockwise b[n-1-j][i] Mirror left ↔ right b[i][n-1-j] Mirror top ↔ bottom b[n-1-i][j] Transpose b[j][i]
Write each transform as "where does cell (i, j) go?". Then 180° = 90° twice, and combinations are transforms applied one after another.
Never rotate in place: writing a[j][n-1-i] while still reading a destroys cells you need. Build the result in a second array, then copy it back (P1205).

C C LANGUAGE · ADDITIONAL INFORMATION In C, a grid of characters is a 2D char array, char g[N][N] , and each row is read with cin >> g[i] or scanf("%s", g[i]) . Leave one extra column for the hidden \0 that ends each row. A whole array cannot be assigned with = , so copying uses memcpy(dst, src, sizeof src) .
runs always start with 0s
Store a 0/1 sequence (a grid read row by row) as the lengths of its runs. By convention the first run counts 0s, so a sequence starting with 1 begins with a run of length 0 (P1319, P1320).
The Luogu problems for this chapter, a ladder through them, and experiments to try yourself.
Key points to memorise
1. int a[N] has a[0] … a[N−1]; size with a margin; big arrays go global.
2. Global arrays start at 0, local ones hold garbage; set values with = {} or fill.
3. (C) memset fills bytes: only 0 and −1 are safe; C grids are char g[N][N], copied with memcpy.
4. Pick 0-based or 1-based once; 1-based leaves index 0 free as padding.
5. Record: mark[p] = 1 handles overlaps; counter: cnt[v]++ tallies values.
6. Negative values: cnt[v + offset]; −100..100 needs 201 boxes.
7. Toggle with ^= 1; counting by value also sorts.
8. All pairs once: for i, for j = i + 1; from j = 0 gives 2 × correct + n.
9. Sliding window: s += a[i] − a[i − m], O(n) instead of O(n·m).
10. a[i][j] = row i, column j; rows outside, columns inside.
11. Recurrence from the row above reads row i − 1; zero padding removes edge cases.
12. dx/dy arrays for moves; turn right with (d + 1) % 4; check bounds first.
13. Rotate 90° clockwise (0-based): b[j][n−1−i] = a[i][j]; never in place.
14. Run-length: runs alternate and start with a run of 0s.
